title: Fighting Fire with Fire: Variolation
summary: Long before modern medicine, healers in China, India, Africa and Turkey tried a brave idea. They gave healthy people a tiny bit of smallpox on purpose, so they would catch a milder case and be safe forever after. It usually worked, but it was still risky.

sections.heading: A Dangerous Idea That Usually Worked
paragraphs: At the end of the last part, we met a puzzle. If surviving smallpox protects you for life, could you catch it on purpose, in a gentler way, and skip the worst danger? It sounds like a frightening idea, a bit like fighting a fire by lighting a small, controlled fire first. Yet for hundreds of years, in many different parts of the world, people did exactly that.

The title of this part borrows an idea from firefighting. When a huge wildfire is coming, firefighters sometimes burn a strip of land on purpose, in a controlled way, so that when the big fire arrives there is nothing left there for it to burn. It sounds backwards, but a small fire that you choose and control can protect you from a giant one you cannot control. Variolation worked on a similar principle, with a small, chosen illness standing in for a big, deadly one.

The method is called variolation. The word comes from 'variola', the Latin-based name for smallpox, so variolation simply means 'smallpoxing' someone. In English it was also often called inoculation. That word has a lovely history of its own. It comes from the Latin 'inoculare', which gardeners used for grafting, when you take a bud from one plant and set it into a cut on another so it grows there. Early writers saw a similarity: a healer took a tiny bit of smallpox material and set it into a small cut in a person's skin, where it 'took' and grew.

Here is how variolation worked. A healer took material from the sores or scabs of someone with smallpox. They then put that material into a healthy person who had never had the disease, either by scratching it into the skin or by blowing powdered scabs into the nose. After a week or two, the person usually became ill with smallpox, but in most cases it was a much milder illness than catching smallpox the ordinary way. They might have a fever and a few dozen spots instead of hundreds. When they recovered, they were protected against smallpox for the rest of their lives, just as if they had survived a natural case.

What did it feel like? Accounts from the 1700s describe a fairly regular timetable. For the first few days after the scratch, almost nothing happened, apart from a little redness and itching where the material had been placed. Around a week later, the person usually developed a fever, a headache and aches, much like the start of natural smallpox. A few days after that, spots appeared, often only a few dozen, with the biggest cluster near the scratch itself. Within two to four weeks of the procedure, most people had recovered and the last scabs were dropping off.

The numbers explain why people were willing to take the risk. Natural variola major killed roughly 30 in every 100 people it infected. Variolation killed roughly 1 or 2 in every 100. It was not safe, but it was far less dangerous than waiting for the next epidemic to arrive.

Why was variolation usually so much milder? Even today, scientists are not completely sure. One idea is that the route mattered. Natural smallpox usually entered through the airways and spread inside the body in a particular way, while variolation put the virus into the skin, where the body's defences may have had a head start. Another idea is that healers often chose material from people with mild cases, which may have helped. The dose may have mattered too: a tiny amount in a scratch is very different from breathing in a sick person's air for days. Probably several of these reasons worked together.

Before going further, it is important to remember that variolation was used only for smallpox and only in the past. It was replaced by much safer methods, which you will meet later in this story. Nothing in this part is a guide to what anyone should do today. It is a story about how people long ago tried to solve a terrifying problem with the knowledge they had.

sections.heading: Powder and a Silver Tube: China
paragraphs: Some of the best-documented early variolation comes from China. There, the most famous method did not involve cutting the skin at all. Instead, healers dried smallpox scabs, ground them into a fine powder and blew it into the nose of the person being protected, through a small blowpipe. This method is called nasal insufflation, which simply means blowing something into the nose.

When did this begin? Chinese stories tell of a much older origin. One tale says that in the late 900s or early 1000s, during the Song dynasty, a powerful official named Wang Dan lost a child to smallpox and searched for a way to protect his other children, until a wise hermit or holy person from a sacred mountain showed his family the secret. It is a good story, but it comes from a book written in the early 1800s (usually dated 1808), roughly 800 years after the events it describes. Historians, including the famous British scholar of Chinese science Joseph Needham, treat it as a legend rather than proven history. It might contain a seed of truth, or it might not; there is no firm evidence either way.

The first reliable written mention appears in the mid-1500s. A doctor named Wan Quan mentioned the practice in a book about smallpox and measles published in 1549, though he did not explain the details. Needham, after studying many old texts, concluded that variolation was spreading widely in China during the reign of the Longqing Emperor, between 1567 and 1572. Through the 1600s, more Chinese doctors wrote about it in their books.

Chinese variolators developed careful rules. They preferred scabs from children who had had mild cases with few spots. They wrapped the scabs in paper, sealed them in a bottle, labelled them with the date and kept them away from sunlight and heat. They noticed that scabs stayed effective longer in cold weather than in hot weather, so they used them within a certain time depending on the season. Some practitioners also aged the scabs for a while before use, which may have weakened the virus a little. The person who had been variolated was kept apart from others until the rash had cleared, because they could spread smallpox to others.

The details of the nose method were precise. Old Chinese descriptions say that three or four dried scabs were ground into powder, sometimes mixed with a grain of musk, a strong-smelling substance used in traditional medicine, and wrapped in a little cotton. The material was packed into the end of a silver blowpipe and puffed up one nostril. There was even a rule about which side: the right nostril was used for boys and the left nostril for girls. Healers believed that fresh scabs were more likely to cause a full-blown, dangerous infection, which is why they preferred scabs that had been left to dry for some time.

Variolation even reached the imperial palace. The Kangxi Emperor, who ruled China from 1661 to 1722, had survived smallpox himself as a child. According to many historians, his survival was one reason he was chosen to become emperor, because he was now protected from the disease that killed so many. Kangxi approved of variolation and had his children inoculated. Accounts say he had soldiers inoculated as well.

News of the Chinese method travelled. In 1700, two separate reports describing it reached the Royal Society in London, Britain's leading scientific club. The members found them interesting, but nobody tried the method in England. The idea had arrived too early, and nobody important was ready to champion it yet.

sections.heading: The Tika Makers of India
paragraphs: In India, variolation used a different technique. Instead of blowing powder into the nose, practitioners made small scratches or needle pricks in the skin, usually on the arm, and rubbed in material from smallpox sores or scabs. In some places the material was mixed with a little water before use.

Our most detailed accounts of Indian variolation come from European visitors in the 1700s. A writer named Oliver Coult described it in 1731. In the late 1760s, a British surgeon named John Zephaniah Holwell, who had lived in Bengal, wrote a longer account. He described travelling inoculators, often Brahmins, members of a priestly group, who moved from village to village before the smallpox season. They followed strict rules about diet and cold baths for the people they inoculated, and they treated the procedure as both medicine and religious ceremony, often with prayers to Sitala, the goddess linked with smallpox.

Another letter from 1768 described two methods used in Bengal: rubbing smallpox material into small pricks in the skin, and, more unusually, giving people scab material to swallow in a little sugar. Practitioners of the skin method were called tikadars. The word 'tika' is still used in many Indian languages today to mean vaccination, a living echo of this old practice.

How old was Indian variolation? Holwell said it had been used for hundreds of years, and some writers have claimed it goes back thousands of years to ancient Sanskrit texts. Modern historians are more cautious. No ancient text clearly describes inoculation, and some scholars have argued that there is no strong reason to assume the practice began in India. The honest answer is that it was well established by the 1700s and was probably older, but its true starting date is unknown.

sections.heading: Buying the Smallpox: Africa
paragraphs: Inoculation against smallpox was also widely practised across Africa, in many different forms. Because most African communities passed knowledge on by speaking and teaching rather than in written books, the oldest records we have mostly come from travellers, doctors and, importantly, from Africans themselves who described the practice to outsiders.

In West Africa, people of many regions knew the technique. It was known, for example, among the Ga-Adangbe people around Accra, in what is now Ghana. The basic method was similar to the Indian one: make a small cut or scratch in the skin and introduce material from a smallpox sore.

In the Sudan region of north-east Africa, travellers recorded a custom with a memorable name. It was called 'tishteree el jidderi', which means 'buying the smallpox'. A mother would take her child to the home of another child who had a mild case. She would tie a strip of cloth around the sick child's arm and then bargain with the family over the price of each pustule. The cloth, carrying the material, was then tied around the arm of the healthy child. A second custom was called 'dak el jedri', or 'hitting the smallpox', in which fluid from a pustule was rubbed into a small cut in the skin. Versions of these practices were still in use in Sudan in the late 1800s.

Notice what these customs have in common with the methods used in China and India. The donor was chosen carefully, usually a child with a mild case. Only a small amount of material was used. And in many African and Ottoman communities the practice was organised by women, especially mothers and older women healers, who passed the knowledge down through families. Across thousands of kilometres, often with little or no direct contact, people had arrived at strikingly similar rules.

The practice also crossed the Atlantic in a way that would change history. Millions of Africans were enslaved and forcibly taken to the Americas, and some of them carried the knowledge of inoculation with them. In the colonies, several enslaved Africans described to curious Europeans how they had been protected as children back home, and showed the marks on their arms. One of them, a man known as Onesimus who lived in Boston, will play a starring role in the next part of this story.

This is an important reminder about how ideas travel. The knowledge that helped bring inoculation to Europe and America did not come only from famous scientists in big cities. Much of it came from ordinary healers, mothers and grandparents in Asia, Africa and the Middle East, whose names were never written down.

sections.heading: The Old Women of Constantinople
paragraphs: In the early 1700s, the Ottoman Empire was one of the great powers of the world. Its capital, Constantinople (today's Istanbul), sat where Europe meets Asia and was full of merchants, diplomats and travellers from many lands. Inoculation was well known there, and it was usually carried out not by doctors but by local women healers, often older women who were experts at the technique.

Where did the Ottomans learn it? The French writer Voltaire, writing in the 1730s, claimed that the Turks had learned inoculation from the Circassians, a people living in the Caucasus mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Some later historians say that Circassian traders brought the practice to the Ottoman Empire around 1670. Like many such origin stories, it is hard to prove, but it shows that people at the time saw inoculation as an idea that had travelled along trade routes.

The Ottoman method was simple. In the cooler months, when smallpox was thought to be less severe, families arranged for an inoculator to visit. She brought material from a mild smallpox case, sometimes carried in a nutshell. She made a few small scratches or pricks with a needle, often on the arms or legs, and placed a tiny drop of the material in each. A few days later the person usually developed a fever and a modest number of spots, rested for a while, and recovered with lifelong protection.

Two doctors helped carry the news from Constantinople to the scientists of Western Europe. The first was Emanuel Timoni, a Greek physician born in 1669 on the island of Chios, whose father had worked as an interpreter at the Sultan's court. Timoni had studied medicine at the universities of Oxford in England and Padua in Italy, then became a physician in Constantinople, including at the Sultan's court. He wrote a letter describing what he had seen of inoculation, and in 1714 it was read to the Royal Society in London and published in the Society's journal, the Philosophical Transactions, one of the oldest science journals in the world.

The second was Giacomo Pylarini, another Greek physician, born in 1659 on the island of Cephalonia. He had studied law and then medicine at Padua, travelled widely, practised medicine in Smyrna (today's İzmir) and Constantinople, and served as the consul, or official representative, of the Republic of Venice in Smyrna. Pylarini wrote his own account of inoculation, published in Latin, and a version of it appeared in the Philosophical Transactions in 1716. Its Latin title promised 'a new and safe method' of giving smallpox by transplanting it from one person to another.

The members of the Royal Society read these reports with interest. They discussed them and printed them. But reading about something and actually doing it are very different things. No English doctor rushed to try it. Inoculation seemed foreign, strange and frightening, and nobody wanted to be the first to deliberately give smallpox to a healthy English child.

sections.heading: The Price of Protection
paragraphs: Variolation saved many lives, but it came with real dangers, and it is important to be honest about them.

The first danger was to the person being inoculated. Variolation gave them an actual smallpox infection, not a pretend one. Usually the case was mild, but sometimes it was not. Roughly 1 or 2 people out of every 100 who were variolated died from the smallpox it caused. Some accounts from different times and places give slightly higher figures, around 2 or 3 in 100. Either way, every family that chose inoculation knew that their healthy child might become seriously ill, or even die, because of a decision they had made.

Let us picture the choice with numbers. Imagine 1,000 children in a city where smallpox returns every few years. If all of them eventually caught natural variola major, around 300 might die. If all of them were variolated, perhaps 10 to 20 might die. Those 10 to 20 are real children, and that is a heartbreaking cost. But it is far smaller than 300. Parents had to weigh a smaller, chosen risk now against a larger, uncertain risk later.

The second danger was to everyone else. A variolated person had real smallpox, so they could pass it on. And the people who caught it from them did not get the gentle, scratched-in version. They caught ordinary smallpox, through the air, with all its usual dangers. One careless inoculation could start a full epidemic among neighbours who had never agreed to take any risk at all.

That is why careful variolators insisted that inoculated people be kept apart from others while they were sick, often for several weeks, until the last scab had fallen off. In China, the inoculated were isolated until the rash cleared. In later centuries, special inoculation houses were built where people stayed until they were no longer contagious. When these rules were broken, outbreaks followed.

Experienced inoculators also learned that timing mattered. Wherever possible, they preferred to inoculate healthy people during calm periods, rather than in the middle of a raging epidemic, when the person might already have caught natural smallpox before the inoculation could protect them. In the Ottoman Empire and in India, inoculation was often arranged for particular seasons, when the disease was thought to be gentler. Healers also tended to avoid people who were already weak or ill. These were rules of thumb, built up from long experience rather than from experiments, but they show how seriously the best practitioners took the risks.

There were other problems too. Variolation could only be done with material from a person who currently had smallpox, so healers needed a constant supply. If the donor had another disease in their blood, that could sometimes be passed on as well. And the process took time, cost money in many places and meant days or weeks of illness. In the end, as you will discover, the risk of variolation spreading smallpox to others was one of the main reasons it was eventually replaced by something much safer and then banned in some countries.

sections.heading: News Travels to a Determined Noblewoman
paragraphs: Let us step back and look at the map. By around 1700, deliberate smallpox inoculation was being practised in China, India, many parts of Africa, the Middle East and the Ottoman Empire. Different cultures used different techniques: powder in the nose, scratches on the arm, cloth tied around a child's limb. But they all rested on the same discovery: a carefully chosen, milder case of smallpox could protect a person for life.

Even in Europe, the idea may not have been completely unknown. A medieval medical text linked to the famous medical school at Salerno in southern Italy mentions putting material from pustules into infants. In Wales, records from near the town of Haverfordwest suggest that ordinary country people were using a form of folk variolation as early as about 1600, long before doctors took any interest. Later in the 1700s, in the remote Shetland Islands north of Scotland, a self-taught man nicknamed Johnnie Notions became famous locally for his careful home-made inoculations. These scattered folk practices show that people in many places, not just in Asia and Africa, had noticed the same clue and acted on it.

None of these healers, in any country, knew what smallpox actually was. Nobody had seen a virus. There was no theory of germs, no idea of an immune system, no laboratory tests. Variolation was built entirely on careful observation and experience, passed from one generation to the next: this works, this is dangerous, this kind of donor is better, keep the sick apart. It is a powerful example of how people can discover something that works long before anyone can explain why it works.

Western Europe was one of the last places to hear about it, and even after the reports from Timoni and Pylarini, it did nothing. What the idea needed was not more evidence on paper. It needed a champion: someone brave and stubborn enough to try it on their own family and then convince others to follow.

In 1717, a new British ambassador arrived in Constantinople with his family. His wife was an intelligent, witty writer from a noble English family. She had survived smallpox only two years earlier. It had left her face scarred and taken away her eyelashes, and the disease had already killed her younger brother. Now, walking the streets of Constantinople and visiting Ottoman households, she was about to see something that would change her life, and the history of medicine in Britain. Her name was Lady Mary Wortley Montagu.

deepDive: Historians of medicine debate two big questions about variolation: where it began, and why it worked as well as it did. On origins, the evidence is patchy and often filtered through outsiders. In China, the first credible written mention is in Wan Quan's 1549 book on smallpox and measles, and Joseph Needham argued that the practice was widespread by the Longqing reign (1567 to 1572). Stories placing it in the 900s or 1000s rest on texts written centuries later, especially an 1808 account of the official Wang Dan, so they are treated as legends. For India, the best descriptions come from Europeans such as Oliver Coult (1731) and John Zephaniah Holwell (late 1760s); claims of an ancient Sanskrit origin are not supported by any clear ancient text, and a 2012 study argued there is no reason to assume India was the source. African practices are even harder to date because they were passed on orally, yet testimony from enslaved West Africans in the Americas in the early 1700s shows the practice was established across a wide region. Many scholars now think variolation may have been invented independently in several places, or spread along trade routes in ways we cannot trace. On mechanism, the key puzzle is why a scratch inoculation usually caused milder disease than natural infection with the same virus. Proposed explanations include the route of entry (skin rather than airways), a small dose, the choice of donors with mild disease, and, in China, ageing of scab material that might have reduced the amount of live virus. The death rate was usually quoted at about 1 to 2 percent, with some sources giving 2 to 3 percent, against roughly 30 percent for natural variola major. But that personal benefit came with a public cost: inoculated people could transmit ordinary smallpox. This tension between individual protection and community risk is a theme that would shape public health debates for centuries, and it is one reason the safer, non-contagious method developed after 1796 replaced variolation so quickly. Britain eventually made variolation illegal in 1840.
funFact: The word 'inoculate' originally came from gardening: it described grafting a bud from one plant into another, and the Latin root 'oculus' means 'eye', the old name for a plant bud.

check.q: Roughly how many variolated people died, compared with about 30 in 100 for natural variola major?
wrong: About 30 in 100, the same as natural smallpox
